content_of_post_to_comment: This is probably a common view of economics. I used to share a few of these but then learned that these criticisms are flawed - one semester of PhD courses will show you why. The main criticism - economics oversimplifies because people don't act like the individuals in our model. Well, it turns out than - on aggregate - people do often act like the individual in our model. We were never trying to model what Jostein would do. We model what the whole country does. And it turns out, often all people together act like in our models. Edit: in my writing, I often cover the limitations of econ research. I also point out the costs/benefits of policies. There's lots to learn from economics and you'd be surprised how little of economics is shown to the public - most likely any question or concern you may have on any social or economic questions has at least been discussed if not formally modelled.
comment: A useful distinction is between models being wrong about individuals and being useful about systems. The harder question is where aggregation breaks—especially when incentives change the behavior being measured.
